'''Tang Dingyuan''' ({{zh|s=汤定元}}; 12 May 1920 – 3 June 2019), also known as '''Ting-Yuan Tang''',<ref name="Hazen1999" /> was a Chinese physicist and writer. He was considered a founder of [[semiconductor]] and [[infrared]] research in China. He served as Director of the Shanghai Institute of Technical Physics and was elected an academician of the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]] in 1991.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Tang Dingyuan zhuan |trans-title=Biography of Tang Dingyuan |chapter=Preface |author=Mi Zhengming 宓正明|publisher=Science Press|year=2011|isbn=9787030301536|location=Beijing|oclc=712855654|language=zh}}</ref>

== Early life ==
Tang was born on 12 May 1920 in [[Jintan District|Jintan]], [[Jiangsu]], Republic of China.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://xw.qq.com/cmsid/20190605A06JX600|title=我国红外学科奠基人汤定元逝世，百岁人生风雨兼程|date=2019-06-05|website=Tencent|access-date=2019-06-07}}</ref> After finishing middle school in Jintan, he entered Wuxi Normal College in 1935. Two years later, however, the [[Second Sino-Japanese War]] broke out and the Japanese army occupied Jiangsu. Tang and his classmates fled [[Wuxi]] and begged their way to [[Wuhan]] in central China, where they lived in a refugee camp.<ref name=":3" /> In 1938, the [[Kuomintang]] government arranged for the student refugees to enroll at National Sichuan High School in [[Chongqing]], China's wartime capital. He subsequently entered [[National Central University]], then also exiled in Chongqing,<ref name=":3" /> and graduated from the Department of Physics in 1942.<ref name=":2" />

== Career in the United States ==
In 1946, after the end of World War II, Tang took the government scholarship examination for studying in the United States, but failed due to his poor English skills. In 1948, he managed to take a loan from National Central University and went to the US on his own expense.<ref name=":3" />

After briefly attending the [[University of Minnesota]], he transferred to the [[University of Chicago]], where he earned his master's degree in physics in 1950 under the supervision of [[Andrew W. Lawson]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite news|url=https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_3595382|script-title=zh:中科院院士汤定元今天上午在上海逝世，享年100岁|author=Yang Fan 杨帆|date=2019-06-03|work=The Paper|access-date=2019-06-05|language=zh}}</ref> At Chicago, he discovered a new [[phase transition]] of the metal [[cerium]] under high pressure and determined that it occurred from the sudden contraction of the [[atomic radius]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://www.hlhl.org.cn/english/showsub.asp?id=448|title=Tang Dingyuan|publisher=Ho Leung Ho Lee Foundation|access-date=2019-06-05}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> With Lawson, he also invented the [[Diamond anvil cell|split diamond bomb]], a device for taking x-rays under high pressure,<ref name="Hazen1999">{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fNJQok6N9_MC&pg=PA216|title=The Diamond Makers|last=Hazen|first=Robert M.|date=1999|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-65474-6|pages=216}}</ref> which became widely used in [[high-pressure physics]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name="Hazen1999" />

== Career in China ==
After the outbreak of the [[Korean War]], Tang gave up his doctoral studies and returned to China in 1951,<ref name=":3" /> where he joined the Institute of Applied Physics of the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="Tan2014">{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FDq7CgAAQBAJ&pg=PA250|title=History of Modern Optics and Optoelectronics Development in China|last=Tan|first=Shouyun|date=2014|publisher=World Scientific|isbn=978-981-4518-77-2|pages=250–1}}</ref> He and [[Wang Shouwu]], also a recent returnee from the US, together built a [[semiconductor]] research group at the institute. After being briefly disrupted by the [[Three-anti and Five-anti Campaigns]] in 1952, they planned to conduct research on the semiconductors [[germanium]] and [[silicon]].<ref name="Tan2014" /> Due to the Western world's embargo against China since the Korean War, however, they were unable to acquire sufficient high-purity material, and decided to work on [[galena]] ([[lead(II) sulfide|PbS]]) and [[copper(I) oxide]] (Cu<sub>2</sub>O) instead.<ref name="Tan2014" /> Tang stumbled upon the property of PbS as an [[infrared detector]], and realized the importance of this property from the visiting Soviet scientist [[Ivan Bardin]].<!-- mistranliterated as Palkim in source, likely from 巴尔金 in Chinese --> Tang's group was the first to conduct infrared research in China.<ref name="Tan2014" />

In 1958, Tang led an infrared detector group with scientists from nine research institutions. In 1964, he became Director of the [[Shanghai Institute of Technical Physics]] and turned it into one of China's top infrared research centers.<ref name=":1" /> He developed about ten infrared or semiconductor devices including the [[silicon solar cell]] and the [[mercury cadmium telluride]] detector, which were used in satellites, missiles, and civilian instruments.<ref name=":1" /> His research led to the development of infrared detectors for the [[PL-2]] [[air-to-air missile]]s<ref name="Tan2014" /> and is considered a major contribution to the [[Two Bombs, One Satellite]] project.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> As his work was highly classified, Tang disappeared from public view for many years.<ref name=":2" />

Tang was elected an academician of the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]] in 1991.<ref name=":2" /> He was awarded the [[Ho Leung Ho Lee Prize]] for Science and Technology Progress, and donated the entire prize money of HK$200,000 to his alma mater, Hua Luogeng High School in Jintan.<ref name=":2" />

Tang published ten [[popular science]] books. In his old age, he frequently gave lectures to schoolchildren, and served as a scientific advisor to a children's science newspaper in Shanghai.<ref name=":2" />

== Health and death ==
When he was 85, Tang underwent a [[gallbladder]] surgery. He died on 3 June 2019 at [[Huadong Hospital]] in Shanghai, at the age of 99.<ref name=":2" />
